cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The new rule will ____ every student. (affect / effect)
cards.back: affect
cards.note: Verb meaning 'to influence'. 'Effect' is usually a noun meaning result: 'the effect of the rule'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Everyone ____ Riya has submitted the form. (accept / except)
cards.back: except
cards.note: 'Except' means 'other than'. 'Accept' means to receive or agree to.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The ____ addressed the school assembly. (principal / principle)
cards.back: principal
cards.note: 'Principal' is the head of a school; also 'main'. 'Principle' is a rule or belief.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The bus remained ____ at the signal. (stationary / stationery)
cards.back: stationary
cards.note: 'Stationary' means not moving. 'Stationery' means pens, paper and writing materials.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The soup and the bread ____ each other well. (complement / compliment)
cards.back: complement
cards.note: 'Complement' means to complete or go well with. 'Compliment' means praise.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Please ____ me what to do next. (advice / advise)
cards.back: advise
cards.note: 'Advise' is the verb. 'Advice' is the noun: 'good advice'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Be ____ about the matter; it is confidential. (discreet / discrete)
cards.back: discreet
cards.note: 'Discreet' means careful and tactful. 'Discrete' means separate and distinct.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: She sought legal ____ before signing. (council / counsel)
cards.back: counsel
cards.note: 'Counsel' means advice (or a lawyer). 'Council' is an elected or advisory body.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Do not ____ your keys again. (lose / loose)
cards.back: lose
cards.note: 'Lose' (verb) means to fail to keep. 'Loose' (adjective) means not tight.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Do you need any ____ information? (farther / further)
cards.back: further
cards.note: 'Further' means additional. 'Farther' is used for physical distance: 'walk farther'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The dog wagged ____ tail. (its / it's)
cards.back: its
cards.note: 'Its' is possessive. 'It's' is the short form of 'it is' or 'it has'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: She is taller ____ her brother. (then / than)
cards.back: than
cards.note: 'Than' is used in comparisons. 'Then' refers to time: 'first this, then that'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: ____ bag is this? (whose / who's)
cards.back: Whose
cards.note: 'Whose' shows possession. 'Who's' is the short form of 'who is' or 'who has'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: He was ____ the captain of the school team. (formally / formerly)
cards.back: formerly
cards.note: 'Formerly' means earlier or in the past. 'Formally' means in an official or proper way.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The teacher tried to ____ a response from the class. (elicit / illicit)
cards.back: elicit
cards.note: 'Elicit' means to draw out. 'Illicit' means illegal or forbidden.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The company is hiring more ____. (personal / personnel)
cards.back: personnel
cards.note: 'Personnel' means staff or employees. 'Personal' means private or individual.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Please ____ to the exit in an orderly manner. (precede / proceed)
cards.back: proceed
cards.note: 'Proceed' means to go ahead. 'Precede' means to come before.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: A storm is ____; stay indoors. (eminent / imminent)
cards.back: imminent
cards.note: 'Imminent' means about to happen. 'Eminent' means distinguished or well known.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The engineer found an ____ solution to the problem. (ingenious / ingenuous)
cards.back: ingenious
cards.note: 'Ingenious' means clever and inventive. 'Ingenuous' means innocent and frank.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The machine ran in a ____ stream all night without a break. (continual / continuous)
cards.back: continuous
cards.note: 'Continuous' means without a break. 'Continual' means happening repeatedly, with pauses.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: She has ____ the loss with great courage. (born / borne)
cards.back: borne
cards.note: 'Borne' (from 'bear') means carried or endured. 'Born' means brought into life.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: They tried to ____ a plan to save water. (device / devise)
cards.back: devise
cards.note: 'Devise' (verb) means to plan or invent. 'Device' (noun) is a gadget or tool.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Take a deep ____ before you begin. (breath / breathe)
cards.back: breath
cards.note: 'Breath' (noun) is the air taken in. 'Breathe' (verb) is the act of taking in air.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: I wonder ____ it will rain today. (weather / whether)
cards.back: whether
cards.note: 'Whether' introduces alternatives. 'Weather' means the state of the atmosphere.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: We had ice cream for ____. (dessert / desert)
cards.back: dessert
cards.note: 'Dessert' is a sweet course at the end of a meal. 'Desert' is dry land, or to abandon.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Please ____ the book on the table. (lay / lie)
cards.back: lay
cards.note: 'Lay' means to put something down and takes an object. 'Lie' means to recline.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: ____ Hindi, she speaks French and Tamil. (Beside / Besides)
cards.back: Besides
cards.note: 'Besides' means in addition to. 'Beside' means next to.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: There are ____ students in class today than yesterday. (fewer / less)
cards.back: fewer
cards.note: Use 'fewer' with countable nouns (students) and 'less' with uncountable nouns (water).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Please ____ that the door is locked before you leave. (assure / ensure)
cards.back: ensure
cards.note: 'Ensure' means to make certain. 'Assure' means to promise someone. 'Insure' is to cover with insurance.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The ____ for the new school has been chosen. (site / sight)
cards.back: site
cards.note: 'Site' is a location. 'Sight' is vision; 'cite' means to quote.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The sun will ____ at six tomorrow. (raise / rise)
cards.back: rise
cards.note: 'Rise' does not take an object. 'Raise' needs an object: 'raise the flag'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Of the two options, I prefer the ____. (later / latter)
cards.back: latter
cards.note: 'Latter' means the second of two things named. 'Later' means after some time.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: It is ____ cold this morning. (quiet / quite)
cards.back: quite
cards.note: 'Quite' means fairly or completely. 'Quiet' means silent.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'each', 'every', 'either' and 'neither' take which kind of verb?
cards.back:
A singular verb.
Wrong: Each of the players have a medal.
Right: Each of the players has a medal.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: a collective noun (committee, team, class) acting as a unit takes which verb?
cards.back:
A singular verb, with 'its'.
Wrong: The committee have made their decision.
Right: The committee has made its decision.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: after 'one of the' + plural noun, which verb is used?
cards.back:
A singular verb, because the subject is 'one'.
Wrong: One of my friends are a doctor.
Right: One of my friends is a doctor.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb. What is the exception?
cards.back:
When the two words together name one thing or idea, the verb is singular.
Wrong: Bread and butter are my usual breakfast.
Right: Bread and butter is my usual breakfast.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: with 'neither...nor' and 'either...or', the verb agrees with which subject?
cards.back:
The subject nearer to the verb.
Wrong: Neither the teacher nor the students was present.
Right: Neither the teacher nor the students were present.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: with 'as well as', 'along with' and 'together with', the verb agrees with which subject?
cards.back:
The first subject, not the phrase that follows.
Wrong: The teacher, along with her students, are going on the trip.
Right: The teacher, along with her students, is going on the trip.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'advice', 'information', 'furniture' and 'news' are uncountable. Can they take a plural form?
cards.back:
No. They have no plural and take a singular verb.
Wrong: She gave me many advices about the exam.
Right: She gave me a lot of advice about the exam.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: when is 'for' used and when is 'since' used?
cards.back:
'Since' marks a point in time; 'for' marks a period of time.
Wrong: I have lived here since ten years.
Right: I have lived here for ten years.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which tense goes with 'since' for an action that began in the past and continues?
cards.back:
The present perfect (or present perfect continuous), not the simple present.
Wrong: He is ill since Monday.
Right: He has been ill since Monday.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which form of 'be' follows 'wish' for an unreal present wish?
cards.back:
'Were' for all persons.
Wrong: I wish I was taller.
Right: I wish I were taller.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: what is the pattern of an unreal present condition (type 2)?
cards.back:
If + past tense, would + base verb; use 'were' for 'be'.
Wrong: If I was you, I will apologise.
Right: If I were you, I would apologise.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'a' or 'an' depends on what?
cards.back:
The sound, not the spelling: 'an' before a vowel sound, 'a' before a consonant sound.
Wrong: He waited for a hour at an university.
Right: He waited for an hour at a university.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which preposition follows 'different'?
cards.back:
'From', not 'than'.
Wrong: Her view is different than mine.
Right: Her view is different from mine.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: meaning 'talk over', 'be present at', 'go into', 'arrive at', do discuss, attend, enter, reach take a preposition?
cards.back:
No. In these senses they are followed directly by the object.
Wrong: We discussed about the problem.
Right: We discussed the problem.
cards.note: Other senses differ: 'attend to' (deal with) and 'enter into' (begin, e.g. an agreement) take a preposition.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'superior', 'inferior', 'senior', 'junior' and 'prefer' take which word before the second item?
cards.back:
'To', not 'than'.
Wrong: This phone is superior than that one.
Right: This phone is superior to that one.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: can a comparative or superlative be formed twice (more + -er)?
cards.back:
No. Use one form only.
Wrong: This book is more better than that one.
Right: This book is better than that one.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which pronoun case follows a preposition?
cards.back:
The objective case: me, him, her, us, them.
Wrong: The secret is between you and I.
Right: The secret is between you and me.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: items in a list must have what kind of form?
cards.back:
The same grammatical form (parallel structure).
Wrong: She likes reading, writing and to swim.
Right: She likes reading, writing and swimming.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'No sooner' is followed by which structure and which conjunction?
cards.back:
Past perfect (inverted) + 'than'.
Wrong: No sooner had he left when it began to rain.
Right: No sooner had he left than it began to rain.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'Hardly' and 'scarcely' are followed by which conjunction?
cards.back:
'When' (or 'before'), not 'than'.
Wrong: Hardly had she entered than the bell rang.
Right: Hardly had she entered when the bell rang.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'many a' is followed by which noun and verb forms?
cards.back:
A singular noun and a singular verb.
Wrong: Many a student have failed this test.
Right: Many a student has failed this test.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: distances, sums of money and periods of time treated as a whole take which verb?
cards.back:
A singular verb.
Wrong: Ten kilometres are a long distance to walk.
Right: Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: names of subjects like Mathematics and Physics, and 'news', take which verb?
cards.back:
A singular verb, despite the -s ending.
Wrong: Mathematics are my favourite subject.
Right: Mathematics is my favourite subject.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do 'the number of' and 'a number of' differ in verb agreement?
cards.back:
'The number of' takes a singular verb; 'a number of' takes a plural verb.
Wrong: The number of students are rising every year.
Right: The number of students is rising every year.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: a participle phrase at the start must describe which noun?
cards.back:
The subject of the main clause that follows it.
Wrong: Having finished the work, the lights were switched off.
Right: Having finished the work, he switched off the lights.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which verb form follows a preposition?
cards.back:
The gerund (-ing form), not the infinitive.
Wrong: She is fond of to sing.
Right: She is fond of singing.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which pronoun case follows 'let'?
cards.back:
The objective case: me, him, her, us, them.
Wrong: Let he and I go.
Right: Let him and me go.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which tense follows 'It is high time'?
cards.back:
The simple past.
Wrong: It is high time we leave.
Right: It is high time we left.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which part of speech modifies a verb?
cards.back:
An adverb (usually -ly), not an adjective.
Wrong: She sings beautiful.
Right: She sings beautifully.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which verb form follows 'would rather'?
cards.back:
The base form without 'to'.
Wrong: I would rather to stay home.
Right: I would rather stay home.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how is the passive voice of the simple past formed?
cards.back:
was/were + the past participle.
Wrong: The letter typed by the secretary yesterday.
Right: The letter was typed by the secretary yesterday.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which preposition follows 'incapable'?
cards.back:
'Of', not 'to' or 'for'.
Wrong: He is incapable to telling a lie.
Right: He is incapable of telling a lie.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which tense shows an action completed before another past action ('by the time ...')?
cards.back:
The past perfect (had + past participle).
Wrong: By the time we arrived, the film started.
Right: By the time we arrived, the film had started.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The Speaker decided to ____ the member for unparliamentary conduct. (censor / censure)
cards.back: censure
cards.note: 'Censure' is to criticise formally; 'censor' is to suppress or cut parts of a text.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: He is so ____ that he believes every rumour. (credible / credulous)
cards.back: credulous
cards.note: 'Credulous' means too ready to believe; 'credible' means believable.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: We need a ____ judge, one with no personal stake in the case. (disinterested / uninterested)
cards.back: disinterested
cards.note: In its traditional sense 'disinterested' means impartial; 'uninterested' means not interested.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Drivers who ____ traffic rules should be fined. (flaunt / flout)
cards.back: flout
cards.note: 'Flout' is to openly disregard a rule; 'flaunt' is to show off.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The poem's last line is an indirect ____ to the Mahabharata. (allusion / illusion)
cards.back: allusion
cards.note: An allusion is an indirect reference; an illusion is a false impression.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The couple decided to ____ an orphaned child. (adapt / adopt)
cards.back: adopt
cards.note: 'Adopt' is to take on legally as one's own; 'adapt' is to adjust.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The club meets on ____ Sundays, that is, every second Sunday. (alternate / alternative)
cards.back: alternate
cards.note: 'Alternate' means every other one; 'alternative' means another possible choice.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: She is my ____, and I tell her every secret. (confidant / confident)
cards.back: confidant
cards.note: A confidant is a person trusted with secrets; 'confident' means self-assured.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The police used tear gas to ____ the crowd. (disburse / disperse)
cards.back: disperse
cards.note: 'Disperse' is to scatter; 'disburse' is to pay out money.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Dense fog began to ____ the whole valley. (envelop / envelope)
cards.back: envelop
cards.note: 'Envelop' is a verb meaning to wrap or cover completely; 'envelope' is the paper cover for a letter.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: A ____ of fans rushed onto the field. (hoard / horde)
cards.back: horde
cards.note: A horde is a large crowd; a hoard is a stored-up supply.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: From the empty chairs we ____ that the meeting had ended. (imply / infer)
cards.back: infer
cards.note: To infer is to conclude from evidence; to imply is to suggest without stating.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: He was ____ to leave without thanking his host. (loath / loathe)
cards.back: loath

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The team's ____ was high after the victory. (moral / morale)
cards.back: morale
cards.note: 'Morale' is the confidence and spirit of a group; 'moral' relates to right and wrong.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The state will ____ the accused for fraud. (prosecute / persecute)
cards.back: prosecute
cards.note: To prosecute is to take legal action against; to persecute is to treat cruelly because of belief or identity.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: He is too ____ to criticism and is easily hurt. (sensible / sensitive)
cards.back: sensitive
cards.note: 'Sensitive' means quick to react or be hurt; 'sensible' means showing good sense.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Parliament passed a ____ to protect wildlife. (statue / statute)
cards.back: statute
cards.note: A statute is a written law passed by a legislature; a statue is a carved figure.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: We drove along a ____ mountain road full of sharp bends. (tortuous / torturous)
cards.back: tortuous
cards.note: 'Tortuous' means full of twists; 'torturous' means causing great pain.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: She doubted the ____ of his claim. (veracity / voracity)
cards.back: veracity
cards.note: Veracity is truthfulness; voracity is greed for food or knowledge.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The bank agreed to ____ the late fee. (wave / waive)
cards.back: waive
cards.note: To waive is to give up a right or requirement; to wave is to move the hand.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Candidates ____ for votes from house to house. (canvas / canvass)
cards.back: canvass
cards.note: To canvass is to seek support or votes; canvas is a heavy cloth.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The President gave his ____ to the bill, and it became law. (ascent / assent)
cards.back: assent
cards.note: Assent is formal agreement; ascent is the act of climbing up.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The listening test checks ____ comprehension. (aural / oral)
cards.back: aural
cards.note: 'Aural' relates to hearing; 'oral' relates to the mouth or speech.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: A ____ conference is held once in two years. (biannual / biennial)
cards.back: biennial
cards.note: 'Biennial' means once every two years; 'biannual' means twice a year.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The fugitive managed to ____ the police for months. (elude / allude)
cards.back: elude
cards.note: To elude is to escape from or avoid; to allude is to refer indirectly.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: A person with no sense of right and wrong at all is ____. (immoral / amoral)
cards.back: amoral
cards.note: 'Amoral' means lacking any moral sense; 'immoral' means breaking moral rules.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: Non-violence is a central ____ of Gandhi's philosophy. (tenant / tenet)
cards.back: tenet
cards.note: A tenet is a principle or belief; a tenant rents property.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The cyclone is expected to ____ havoc on the coast. (wreak / reek)
cards.back: wreak
cards.note: 'Wreak havoc' is the fixed phrase; to reek is to smell strongly.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: To ____ should the letter be addressed? (who / whom)
cards.back: whom
cards.note: Use 'whom' as the object of a verb or preposition: 'to whom'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The law demands ____ treatment of animals. (human / humane)
cards.back: humane
cards.note: 'Humane' means showing kindness and compassion; 'human' relates to people.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The government issued an ____ because Parliament was not in session. (ordinance / ordnance)
cards.back: ordinance
cards.note: An ordinance is a law made by executive order; ordnance means military weapons and supplies.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: His rude remark at the meeting was most ____. (regretful / regrettable)
cards.back: regrettable
cards.note: 'Regrettable' describes what causes regret; 'regretful' describes a person who feels it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Choose the correct word: The valley was covered with ____ vegetation after the monsoon. (luxurious / luxuriant)
cards.back: luxuriant
cards.note: 'Luxuriant' means lush and thick in growth; 'luxurious' means expensive and comfortable.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: what is the pattern of a real future condition (type 1)?
cards.back:
If + simple present, will + base verb.
Wrong: If it will rain, we will cancel the picnic.
Right: If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: what is the pattern of an unreal past condition (type 3)?
cards.back:
If + past perfect, would have + past participle.
Wrong: If she had studied, she would pass.
Right: If she had studied, she would have passed.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which tense follows 'when', 'before' or 'as soon as' for a future event?
cards.back:
The simple present, not 'will'.
Wrong: I will call you when I will reach home.
Right: I will call you when I reach home.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which verb form follows 'has', 'have' or 'had'?
cards.back:
The past participle (gone, written, taken), not the simple past.
Wrong: He has went to Delhi.
Right: He has gone to Delhi.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'unless' already means 'if not'. What follows it?
cards.back:
An affirmative verb.
Wrong: Unless you don't work hard, you will fail.
Right: Unless you work hard, you will fail.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which auxiliary follows 'lest'?
cards.back:
'Should' (or the bare subjunctive), never 'will' or 'would'.
Wrong: Run fast lest you will miss the train.
Right: Run fast lest you should miss the train.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which conjunction pairs with 'neither', and which with 'either'?
cards.back:
'Neither' pairs with 'nor'; 'either' pairs with 'or'.
Wrong: Neither Ravi or his sister attended.
Right: Neither Ravi nor his sister attended.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: when a sentence begins with 'Not only', what happens to the word order?
cards.back:
The auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion).
Wrong: Not only she sings, but she also dances.
Right: Not only does she sing, but she also dances.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: when 'seldom', 'rarely' or 'never' begins a sentence, what happens to the word order?
cards.back:
The auxiliary comes before the subject.
Wrong: Seldom she visits her village.
Right: Seldom does she visit her village.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which verb form follows 'used to' for a past habit?
cards.back:
The base form of the verb.
Wrong: She used to walking to school.
Right: She used to walk to school.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'such' or 'so' before 'a/an + adjective + noun'?
cards.back:
'Such'; 'so' goes directly before an adjective.
Wrong: It was so a beautiful day.
Right: It was such a beautiful day.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'too' suggests an unwanted excess. Can it replace 'very' in a happy statement?
cards.back:
No. Use 'very'.
Wrong: I am too glad to see you.
Right: I am very glad to see you.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which verb form follows 'cannot help' (meaning 'cannot stop oneself')?
cards.back:
The gerund (-ing form).
Wrong: I could not help to laugh.
Right: I could not help laughing.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which tense goes with 'yesterday', 'ago' or 'last week'?
cards.back:
The simple past, not the present perfect.
Wrong: I have seen him yesterday.
Right: I saw him yesterday.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: can 'know', 'believe', 'want' and 'understand' be used in the continuous tense?
cards.back:
No. These stative verbs take the simple tense.
Wrong: I am knowing the answer.
Right: I know the answer.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: do the possessive pronouns 'hers', 'ours', 'yours' and 'theirs' take an apostrophe?
cards.back:
No. They never take an apostrophe.
Wrong: The red bag is her's.
Right: The red bag is hers.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which preposition goes with a date or a day: 'in', 'on' or 'at'?
cards.back:
'On' (on 5 May, on Monday); 'in' goes with months and years, 'at' with clock time.
Wrong: She was born in 5 May 2004.
Right: She was born on 5 May 2004.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: can 'despite' be followed by 'of'?
cards.back:
No. Say 'despite' or 'in spite of'.
Wrong: Despite of the rain, the match went on.
Right: Despite the rain, the match went on.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: do 'resemble' and 'marry' take a preposition before the object?
cards.back:
No. Both take a direct object.
Wrong: She resembles to her mother.
Right: She resembles her mother.
Wrong: He married with a doctor.
Right: He married a doctor.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: in a comparison, what must be compared with what?
cards.back:
Like with like; use 'that of' or 'those of' to avoid comparing a thing with a place.
Wrong: The climate of Shimla is cooler than Delhi.
Right: The climate of Shimla is cooler than that of Delhi.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'the poor', 'the rich' and 'the young' take which kind of verb?
cards.back:
A plural verb, because they mean groups of people.
Wrong: The poor is often ignored.
Right: The poor are often ignored.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'police', 'cattle' and 'people' take which kind of verb?
cards.back:
A plural verb, though they do not end in -s.
Wrong: The police has arrested the thief.
Right: The police have arrested the thief.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how is a question tag formed after a positive statement?
cards.back:
A negative tag repeating the auxiliary and the pronoun.
Wrong: He is honest, isn't it?
Right: He is honest, isn't he?

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: what word order does a reported question use?
cards.back:
Statement order, with no 'do' support and no question mark.
Wrong: He asked me where was I going.
Right: He asked me where I was going.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: in 'There is/are ...', the verb agrees with which word?
cards.back:
The noun that follows the verb.
Wrong: There is many reasons for the delay.
Right: There are many reasons for the delay.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which verb form follows 'had better'?
cards.back:
The base form without 'to'.
Wrong: You had better to leave now.
Right: You had better leave now.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: which verb form follows 'make' and 'let' with an object (active voice)?
cards.back:
The bare infinitive, without 'to'.
Wrong: The film made me to cry.
Right: The film made me cry.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: 'more than one' is followed by which noun and verb forms?
cards.back:
A singular noun and a singular verb.
Wrong: More than one student were absent.
Right: More than one student was absent.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a factual passage in a reading test?
cards.back: A passage that gives information about real people, events, places or ideas, such as a news report or a science article. Its aim is to inform, and its details can be checked.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the main idea of a passage?
cards.back: The central point the writer wants to make about the topic. Every paragraph supports it, and it is best stated as a full sentence.
cards.note: Topic: 'Pollution'. Main idea: 'Pollution in our rivers can be reduced if towns treat their waste.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the topic of a passage?
cards.back: The subject the passage is about, given in a word or short phrase. It says what the passage covers, not what the writer says about it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a supporting detail?
cards.back: A fact, example, reason or description that backs up or explains the main idea.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a topic sentence?
cards.back: The sentence that states the main idea of a paragraph. It often comes first, but it can also appear in the middle or at the end.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an inference in reading?
cards.back: A conclusion you reach by joining clues in the text with what you already know. The text does not state it directly.
cards.note: 'Rahul pulled his raincoat tighter.' We infer it is raining or cold.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a fact?
cards.back: A statement that can be checked and shown to be true or false, for example by records, measurement or observation.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an opinion?
cards.back: A view or judgement that a person holds. It cannot be proved true or false, and it often uses words such as 'best', 'should' or 'I think'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a claim in a passage?
cards.back: A statement the writer puts forward as true and tries to prove with reasons and evidence.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is evidence in a passage?
cards.back: The facts, examples, figures or expert statements a writer uses to show that a claim is true.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is bias in writing?
cards.back: A strong leaning for or against a person, group or idea, which makes the writing one-sided and unfair.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is objective writing?
cards.back: Writing based on facts and kept free of the writer's personal feelings or opinions. It stays neutral.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is subjective writing?
cards.back: Writing shaped by the writer's own feelings, tastes and opinions rather than by facts alone.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a context clue?
cards.back: A hint in the words or sentences around an unfamiliar word that helps you work out its meaning.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is expository writing?
cards.back: Writing that explains or gives information about a subject, as in a textbook chapter or a how-to article. Its aim is to inform and explain.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is persuasive writing?
cards.back: Writing that tries to make the reader believe something or act in a certain way, using reasons, appeals and strong language. An advertisement is an example.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is argumentative writing?
cards.back: Writing that takes a position on an issue and backs it with logical reasons and evidence, often answering the opposite view as well.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is descriptive writing?
cards.back: Writing that paints a clear picture of a person, place, object or event through vivid details that appeal to the senses.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Types of text structure in a factual passage
cards.back:
Description: details about a person, place, thing or idea
Sequence: events or steps in time order
Cause and effect: why something happens and what follows
Compare and contrast: how things are alike and different
Problem and solution: a problem and the ways to deal with it

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Types of author's purpose
cards.back:
To inform: give facts and knowledge
To explain: show how or why something works
To persuade: win the reader over to a view or action
To entertain: amuse or interest the reader
To describe: paint a picture of a person, place or thing

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Types of context clue
cards.back:
Definition clue: the sentence states the meaning, often after 'is', 'means' or a comma
Synonym clue: a word of similar meaning appears nearby
Antonym clue: an opposite word nearby, often after 'but' or 'unlike'
Example clue: examples that show the meaning, often after 'such as'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Fact vs opinion: the difference
cards.back:
Fact: a statement that can be checked and proved true or false.
Opinion: a statement of what someone thinks or feels; it cannot be proved.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Main idea vs supporting detail: the difference
cards.back:
Main idea: the central point the whole passage makes.
Supporting detail: a fact, example or reason that backs up that point.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Topic vs main idea: the difference
cards.back:
Topic: the subject of the passage, in a word or phrase ('Water saving').
Main idea: what the writer says about that subject, in a sentence ('Households can save water by fixing leaks').

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Skimming vs scanning: the difference
cards.back:
Skimming: reading quickly to get the general idea of the passage.
Scanning: moving your eyes over the text to find one particular word, name, date or fact.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Summary vs paraphrase: the difference
cards.back:
Summary: a short account of only the main points, in your own words.
Paraphrase: a restatement of the full meaning of a passage in different words; it is about as long as the original.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Stated fact vs inference: the difference
cards.back:
Stated fact: the text says it in so many words.
Inference: the text does not say it, but its clues lead you to it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'therefore' show in a passage?
cards.back: Effect or result: what follows from the reason just given.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'consequently' show in a passage?
cards.back: Effect or result: what happened because of the earlier event.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'however' show in a passage?
cards.back: Contrast: the idea that follows goes against the one before it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'nevertheless' show in a passage?
cards.back: Contrast: something still holds true in spite of what was just said.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'whereas' show in a passage?
cards.back: Contrast: it sets two things side by side to show how they differ.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'similarly' show in a passage?
cards.back: Comparison: the next idea is like the one before it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'for instance' show in a passage?
cards.back: Example: it introduces a case that illustrates the point.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'in addition' show in a passage?
cards.back: Addition: it adds one more point to what has been said.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Which relationship does the signal word 'on the contrary' show in a passage?
cards.back: Contrast: it says the opposite of what was just stated is true.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Fact or opinion: 'The Brahmaputra flows through Assam.'
cards.back:
Fact
It can be checked on a map.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Fact or opinion: 'Cricket is the most exciting sport in the world.'
cards.back:
Opinion
'Most exciting' is a personal judgement.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Fact or opinion: 'Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.'
cards.back:
Fact
It can be tested and measured.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Fact or opinion: 'Everyone should learn to swim before the age of ten.'
cards.back:
Opinion
'Should' shows what the writer thinks is right.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Fact or opinion: 'The school library has more than 4,000 books.'
cards.back:
Fact
The number can be checked by counting.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Fact or opinion: 'Winter mornings are the most peaceful time of the year.'
cards.back:
Opinion
'Most peaceful' depends on feeling; it cannot be proved.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the text structure: 'First, wash the rice. Next, boil it for ten minutes. Finally, drain the water.'
cards.back:
Sequence (chronological order)
The steps come in time order, marked by first, next and finally.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the text structure: 'Because the river was polluted, the fish died, and the fishing families lost their income.'
cards.back:
Cause and effect
A cause (pollution) leads to effects (dead fish, lost income).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the text structure: 'Buses are cheaper than trains, but trains are faster and more comfortable.'
cards.back:
Compare and contrast
Two things are set side by side to show how they differ.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the text structure: 'Many students sleep too little. Schools can help by starting classes an hour later.'
cards.back:
Problem and solution
A problem is stated, then a way to deal with it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a main idea or central theme question?
cards.back:
Ask what every paragraph is about and what the writer wants you to remember. Choose the option that covers the whole passage.
Trap: an option true of one paragraph only, or one too broad.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a suitable title question?
cards.back:
Choose the title that sums up the whole passage in few words: its topic and the writer's point.
Trap: a title naming one detail, or one too wide.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a specific detail question?
cards.back:
Find the question's key words in the passage and read the lines around them. Match the option to the text, not to what you already know.
Trap: an option using the right words with a changed meaning.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a vocabulary in context (meaning, synonym or antonym of a word) question?
cards.back:
Go back to the word and read the sentence around it. Put each option in its place and keep the one that fits. For an antonym, pick the opposite of that sense.
Trap: the common meaning may not be the one used here.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a NOT or EXCEPT question?
cards.back:
Three options are true to the passage and one is not. Check each option against the text, cross out the true ones and choose the one left.
Trap: forgetting the NOT and picking a true statement.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a statement-set ('Which of the statements are true?') question?
cards.back:
Test each statement on its own against the passage and mark it true or false. Then pick the option that matches your marks.
Trap: a statement that is partly true; one wrong word makes it false.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a figure of speech?
cards.back: A word or phrase used in a non-literal way to create a special effect, such as a simile, a metaphor or hyperbole.
cards.note: Saying 'I am starving' does not mean the speaker is dying of hunger.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a simile?
cards.back: A figure of speech that compares two unlike things directly, using 'like' or 'as'.
cards.note: Example: Her voice was as sweet as honey.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a metaphor?
cards.back: A figure of speech that describes one thing by saying it is another, without using 'like' or 'as'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an extended metaphor?
cards.back: A metaphor that is carried on through several lines, or a whole poem or passage, with further details that keep developing the comparison.
cards.note: Example: Life is a road with sharp turns, steep hills and a final destination.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is personification?
cards.back: A figure of speech that gives human qualities, feelings or actions to an object, an animal or an idea.
cards.note: Example: The sun smiled down on the village.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is hyperbole?
cards.back: Deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis or effect, not meant to be taken literally.
cards.note: Example: This bag weighs a ton.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is understatement?
cards.back: Presenting something as smaller, less serious or less important than it really is, often for humour or irony.
cards.note: Example: After the marathon, he said he was 'a little tired'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is alliteration?
cards.back: The repetition of the same consonant sound at the beginning of words that are close together.
cards.note: Example: Fresh flowers filled the field.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is assonance?
cards.back: The repetition of the same vowel sound in nearby words, with different consonant sounds around it.
cards.note: Example: Try to light the white kite.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is consonance?
cards.back: The repetition of the same consonant sound within or at the end of nearby words, with different vowel sounds.
cards.note: Example: 'blank' and 'think' repeat the final 'k' sound.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is onomatopoeia?
cards.back: The use of a word that imitates the sound it names.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an oxymoron?
cards.back: A figure of speech that joins two words of opposite meaning in one phrase.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a paradox?
cards.back: A statement that seems to contradict itself or to be absurd but turns out to contain a truth.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is irony?
cards.back: The use of words or events so that the real meaning or outcome is the opposite of, or very different from, what is said or expected.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is verbal irony?
cards.back: Irony in which a speaker says the opposite of what they really mean.
cards.note: Example: Saying 'What lovely weather!' in the middle of a storm.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is situational irony?
cards.back: Irony in which the outcome of events is the opposite of what was expected or would be fitting.
cards.note: Example: A fire station burns down.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is dramatic irony?
cards.back: Irony in which the audience or reader knows something important that the characters in the story do not.
cards.note: Example: We know the box holds a snake, but the heroine opens it happily.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is satire?
cards.back: A work or style that uses humour, exaggeration or irony to expose and criticise the foolishness or faults of people, institutions or society.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an allegory?
cards.back: A story, poem or picture in which characters and events stand for deeper ideas, usually moral or political ones.
cards.note: Example: George Orwell's Animal Farm stands for the Russian Revolution and what followed.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an allusion?
cards.back: A brief, indirect reference to a person, place, event or work of literature, history or myth that the reader is expected to know.
cards.note: Example: 'He met his Waterloo' alludes to Napoleon's final defeat.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is apostrophe as a figure of speech?
cards.back: Speaking directly to an absent or dead person, or to an object or an idea, as if it could hear and answer.
cards.note: Example: O wind, carry my message home.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is anaphora?
cards.back: The repetition of the same word or phrase at the beginning of successive lines, sentences or clauses.
cards.note: Example: Every day, every night, every hour, she waited.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is antithesis?
cards.back: The placing of sharply contrasting ideas side by side in balanced, parallel phrases or clauses.
cards.note: Example: We want peace; they want war.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is litotes?
cards.back: A form of understatement that affirms something by denying its opposite.
cards.note: Example: 'He is no fool' means he is quite clever.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is metonymy?
cards.back: A figure of speech in which a thing is called by the name of something closely associated with it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is synecdoche?
cards.back: A figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole, or the whole stands for a part.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a pun?
cards.back: A play on words that uses the two meanings of a word, or two words that sound alike, for humour or effect.
cards.note: Example: I wondered why the ball kept getting bigger, and then it hit me.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is imagery in a poem or passage?
cards.back: Descriptive language that appeals to the senses and creates pictures or sensations in the reader's mind.
cards.note: Example: the scent of wet earth and the cold bite of the wind.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is symbolism?
cards.back: The use of an object, person, colour or action to stand for an idea beyond its literal meaning.
cards.note: Example: A dove stands for peace.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a transferred epithet?
cards.back: A figure of speech in which an adjective is moved from the person it really describes to a noun it cannot literally describe.
cards.note: Example: 'An angry letter' means the writer, not the letter, is angry.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a rhetorical question?
cards.back: A question asked to make a point or create an effect, not to get an answer.
cards.note: Example: Can anyone say that war is a good thing?

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is repetition as a literary device?
cards.back: The repeating of a word, phrase or line for emphasis, rhythm or effect.
cards.note: Example: She waited and waited and waited.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a refrain in a poem or song?
cards.back: A line or group of lines repeated at regular intervals, often at the end of each stanza.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is rhyme in poetry?
cards.back: The repetition of the same or a very similar sound at the end of words, usually at the ends of lines.
cards.note: Example: moon and soon; light and night.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is internal rhyme?
cards.back: Rhyme between words inside the same line, or between a word in the middle of a line and the word at its end.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a rhyme scheme?
cards.back: The pattern of end rhymes in a poem, shown by letters, with each new end sound given the next letter.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is rhythm in poetry?
cards.back: The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables that gives a line of verse its beat.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a stanza?
cards.back: A group of lines in a poem that forms one unit, set apart by a space, like a paragraph in prose.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a couplet?
cards.back: Two successive lines of verse, usually of the same length and often rhyming.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a quatrain?
cards.back: A stanza or poem of four lines, which may use any rhyme scheme.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is enjambment?
cards.back: The continuation of a sentence or phrase from one line of verse to the next without a pause or punctuation at the line end.
cards.note: The opposite is an end-stopped line, where the thought ends with the line.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a sonnet?
cards.back: A poem of fourteen lines with a fixed rhyme scheme, usually in iambic pentameter.
cards.note: Two main types: the Petrarchan (Italian) and the Shakespearean (English).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is free verse?
cards.back: Poetry that has no regular rhyme scheme and no fixed metre; its rhythm follows natural speech.
cards.note: Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass is a famous early example.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is blank verse?
cards.back: Poetry written in a regular metre, usually iambic pentameter, but without rhyme.
cards.note: Much of Shakespeare's drama and Milton's Paradise Lost is in blank verse.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an ode?
cards.back: A long lyric poem in a formal, elevated style that is addressed to, and praises, a person, an object or an idea.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a ballad?
cards.back: A poem or song that tells a story in short stanzas, often with a refrain.
cards.note: Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' is a literary ballad.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a lyric poem?
cards.back: A short poem in which a single speaker expresses personal thoughts and feelings.
cards.note: Sonnets and odes are kinds of lyric poems.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an epic in literature?
cards.back: A long narrative poem, in an elevated style, about the heroic deeds of a hero or heroes and important to a nation or culture.
cards.note: Examples: the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and Homer's Iliad.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the speaker of a poem?
cards.back: The voice that talks in the poem. It is a persona created by the poet and is not always the poet.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Types of irony
cards.back:
Verbal irony: the speaker says the opposite of what is meant.
Situational irony: the outcome is the opposite of what was expected.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows something the characters do not.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Types of imagery
cards.back:
Visual imagery: appeals to sight.
Auditory imagery: appeals to hearing.
Tactile imagery: appeals to touch.
Olfactory imagery: appeals to smell.
Gustatory imagery: appeals to taste.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Simile vs metaphor: the difference
cards.back:
Simile: compares two things using 'like' or 'as' (She is as brave as a lion).
Metaphor: says one thing is another, with no 'like' or 'as' (She is a lion in battle).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Metonymy vs synecdoche: the difference
cards.back:
Metonymy: names a thing by something closely associated with it ('the crown' for a king).
Synecdoche: names a thing by one of its parts, or a part by the whole ('hands' for workers).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Alliteration vs assonance: the difference
cards.back:
Alliteration: repeats a consonant sound at the start of nearby words (bright blue boats).
Assonance: repeats a vowel sound inside nearby words (go slow over the road).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Personification vs apostrophe: the difference
cards.back:
Personification: gives human qualities to a non-human thing ('The wind sang').
Apostrophe: speaks directly to an absent person or a thing as if it could answer ('O wind, sing to me').

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Free verse vs blank verse: the difference
cards.back:
Free verse: no regular rhyme and no fixed metre.
Blank verse: no rhyme, but a regular metre, usually iambic pentameter (ten syllables, five beats).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'The little boy ran down the corridor like a startled deer.'
cards.back:
Simile
The boy is compared to a deer directly, using the word 'like'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'The classroom was a zoo before the teacher arrived.'
cards.back:
Metaphor
The classroom is said to be a zoo, with no 'like' or 'as'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'The angry sea refused to let the little boat go.'
cards.back:
Personification
A sea cannot be angry or refuse; it is given human feelings and choices.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'I have told you a million times to close the door.'
cards.back:
Hyperbole
The number is an obvious exaggeration, used for emphasis.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'Bright blue balloons bobbed above the busy bazaar.'
cards.back:
Alliteration
The consonant sound 'b' is repeated at the start of nearby words.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'The kettle hissed and the door banged shut.'
cards.back:
Onomatopoeia
'Hissed' and 'banged' imitate the sounds they name.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'The room fell into a deafening silence.'
cards.back:
Oxymoron
'Deafening' and 'silence' are opposites joined in one phrase.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'O Moon, keep watch over my sleeping child tonight.'
cards.back:
Apostrophe
The speaker addresses the Moon directly, as if it could listen.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'We shall work for peace; we shall work for justice; we shall work for freedom.'
cards.back:
Anaphora
The phrase 'we shall work for' is repeated at the start of each clause.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'Money can buy a house, but not a home.'
cards.back:
Antithesis
Two contrasting ideas, a house and a home, are set in balanced parallel phrases.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'Grandfather passed away peacefully last night.'
cards.back:
Euphemism
'Passed away' is a gentler phrase used in place of 'died'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'The White House announced a new policy today.'
cards.back:
Metonymy
The building stands for the President and the government linked with it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'The farmer hired ten hands for the harvest.'
cards.back:
Synecdoche
'Hands', a part of the workers, stands for the whole workers.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'The baker quit because he could not make enough dough.'
cards.back:
Pun
'Dough' plays on two meanings: bread mixture and money.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'He spent a sleepless night worrying about the result.'
cards.back:
Transferred epithet
'Sleepless' really describes the man, but it is attached to the night.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Name the figure of speech: 'Is there anyone who does not love the monsoon?'
cards.back:
Rhetorical question
It is asked to make a point, and no answer is expected.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the rhyme scheme of these lines? 'The moon is high, / The path is long, / The owls cry, / A soft night song.'
cards.back:
abab
High and cry rhyme (a); long and song rhyme (b).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the rhyme scheme of these lines? 'The stars come out, / The owls shout, / The night grows deep, / The children sleep.'
cards.back:
aabb
Out and shout rhyme (a); deep and sleep rhyme (b).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you find the rhyme scheme of a poem?
cards.back:
Read the lines aloud. Mark the end sound of line 1 as a.
Give each later line the same letter if its end sound matches an earlier one, or the next new letter (b, c ...) if it is new.
Trap: judge by sound, not spelling (love and move do not rhyme).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a central idea question on a poem or extract?
cards.back:
Read the whole poem or extract first, then ask what the writer is saying about the subject overall.
Choose the option that covers the whole text, not one detail.
Trap: an option true of one line only, or one that adds ideas the text does not state.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a question on the meaning of a line or image?
cards.back:
Re-read the line with the lines before and after it. Decide what it stands for beyond its literal sense, such as a comparison, a symbol or a sense picture.
Choose the option that fits the whole poem.
Trap: picking the literal meaning of a figurative line.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a question on the speaker's attitude in a poem?
cards.back:
Find the words, images and details that show how the speaker feels about the subject.
Decide whether the feeling is positive, negative or neutral, then pick the option that fits the whole poem.
Trap: mixing up the poet with the speaker; use only what the text shows.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is tone in a passage?
cards.back: The writer's attitude towards the subject or the reader, shown through word choice, details and style.
cards.note: The same event can sound proud, bitter or amused, depending on the words chosen.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Tone vs mood: the difference
cards.back:
Tone: the writer's attitude towards the subject, such as mocking or admiring.
Mood: the feeling the passage creates in the reader, such as gloomy or calm.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you answer a tone or attitude question?
cards.back:
Mark the words and details that carry feeling: adjectives, verbs, images and punctuation.
Decide positive, negative or neutral first, then pick the exact word.
Check that the option fits the whole passage.
Trap: a word that fits one sentence but not the passage.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Rule: how do you choose between two close tone options?
cards.back:
Compare them by kind and strength: serious or playful, sincere or mocking, mild or strong.
Go back to the passage and match the strength of its language.
Trap: choosing an extreme word such as 'scornful' when the passage is only mildly critical.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'sardonic' tone show?
cards.back: Mocking in a bitter, grimly amused way; the writer sneers at something while seeming to find it funny.
cards.note: Example: 'How generous of the council to repair one pothole in a decade,' he wrote.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'sarcastic' tone show?
cards.back: Saying the opposite of what is meant in order to mock or hurt someone.
cards.note: Example: 'Great, another delay,' she said, after waiting two hours.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'satirical' tone show?
cards.back: Using humour, exaggeration or ridicule to expose and criticise foolishness or wrongdoing, especially in public life.
cards.note: Satire aims to criticise, not just to amuse.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'wry' tone show?
cards.back: Dry, mildly mocking humour that shows the writer finds a bad or awkward situation slightly funny.
cards.note: Example: 'The bus, true to form, arrived just as I finished walking.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'nostalgic' tone show?
cards.back: Fondly longing for a happy time in the past and remembering it with warm feeling.
cards.note: Example: 'Those long summer evenings in the village feel like another world now.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'wistful' tone show?
cards.back: Gently and sadly longing for something that is past or out of reach.
cards.note: Example: 'She watched the train leave, wishing she were on it.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'melancholic' tone show?
cards.back: Deeply and thoughtfully sad, with a lasting gloom that often has no single clear cause.
cards.note: Example: 'The empty playground held nothing but the autumn wind.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'sombre' tone show?
cards.back: Serious, dark and gloomy; a heavy, grave mood with no cheer.
cards.note: Example: 'The mourners stood in silence under a grey sky.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'solemn' tone show?
cards.back: Serious and dignified, without any humour; suited to an important or formal occasion.
cards.note: Example: 'He rose and, in a quiet, measured voice, took the oath.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'reverent' tone show?
cards.back: Showing deep respect and awe for someone or something held sacred or great.
cards.note: Example: 'Pilgrims entered the shrine with bowed heads and hushed voices.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'laudatory' tone show?
cards.back: Praising someone or something warmly and openly.
cards.note: Example: 'Her brilliant work has set a standard for the whole field.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'critical' tone show?
cards.back: Pointing out faults and expressing disapproval of someone or something.
cards.note: Example: 'The plan is poorly thought out and ignores the needs of the poor.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'didactic' tone show?
cards.back: Meant to teach, especially to give a moral lesson, and often in a preachy way.
cards.note: Example: 'Remember, children, honesty is always the best policy.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'cautionary' tone show?
cards.back: Giving a warning so that readers will avoid a danger or mistake.
cards.note: Example: 'Those who ignore the signs of erosion will lose their fields.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'pessimistic' tone show?
cards.back: Expecting the worst; seeing mainly the bad side and doubting that things will improve.
cards.note: Example: 'Nothing will change; these plans always fail in the end.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'resigned' tone show?
cards.back: Accepting something unpleasant because it cannot be changed, without protest.
cards.note: Example: 'The shop would close; there was nothing more to be done.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'scornful' tone show?
cards.back: Showing strong contempt; treating someone or something as worthless.
cards.note: Example: 'He dismissed the idea as the dream of a fool.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'derisive' tone show?
cards.back: Mocking in a jeering way that treats someone as unworthy of respect.
cards.note: Example: 'The crowd roared with jeering laughter at his speech.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'condescending' tone show?
cards.back: Talking down to others as if one is superior, showing they are less clever or important.
cards.note: Example: 'Don't worry, dear, the grown-ups will explain it simply for you.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'patronising' tone show?
cards.back: Seeming kind or friendly while showing that you think the other person is less intelligent or capable.
cards.note: Example: 'Well done for trying; it must be hard for someone like you.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'mocking' tone show?
cards.back: Making fun of someone or something in an unkind way, often by ridiculing or imitating.
cards.note: Example: 'Oh yes, our great leader, the master of all he surveys!'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'jocular' tone show?
cards.back: Playful and joking; cheerful, light humour.
cards.note: Example: 'I would offer you a seat, but the cat has the best one.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'flippant' tone show?
cards.back: Treating something serious without proper respect or seriousness; too casual.
cards.note: Example: 'The exam? Oh, I just guessed my way through it.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'facetious' tone show?
cards.back: Joking about a serious matter in a silly or inappropriate way, at the wrong moment.
cards.note: Example: 'The flood? Just a free swimming pool for the neighbourhood.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'sentimental' tone show?
cards.back: Showing tender feelings such as love, pity or nostalgia, often more than the situation needs.
cards.note: Example: 'Tears filled her eyes as she kissed the faded photograph.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'sympathetic' tone show?
cards.back: Showing understanding and care for another person's suffering or feelings.
cards.note: Example: 'It must have been so hard for you, and I am sorry you went through it.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'detached' tone show?
cards.back: Not emotionally involved; keeping a distance and showing no personal feeling.
cards.note: Example: 'The doctor noted the symptoms, recorded the date and moved to the next patient.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'dispassionate' tone show?
cards.back: Calm and not influenced by strong emotion, so able to be rational and fair.
cards.note: Example: 'Weighing the evidence calmly, the committee reached its verdict.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'bitter' tone show?
cards.back: Angry and resentful because of unfair treatment or disappointment.
cards.note: Example: 'After years of broken promises, he wanted nothing more to do with them.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'reflective' tone show?
cards.back: Thinking deeply and quietly about experiences or ideas.
cards.note: Example: 'Looking back, I see how much that failure taught me.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'conciliatory' tone show?
cards.back: Meant to calm anger and make peace; willing to settle a dispute.
cards.note: Example: 'Perhaps we were both at fault, and I am ready to talk it over.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'defiant' tone show?
cards.back: Openly refusing to obey or give in to authority or opposition; boldly resistant.
cards.note: Example: 'Order me to stop if you like; I will keep speaking.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'caustic' tone show?
cards.back: Severely critical or sarcastic in a biting way that stings.
cards.note: Example: 'A masterpiece, if you enjoy watching paint dry.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What attitude does a 'disparaging' tone show?
cards.back: Expressing the view that something is of little value or importance; belittling.
cards.note: Example: 'It was merely a small effort, hardly worth a mention.'

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a narrative passage?
cards.back: A passage that tells a story or an account of events, usually in time order, with characters, a setting and some problem or change.
cards.note: Typical clues: named characters, past-tense events, dialogue and a sequence of happenings.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the plot of a story?
cards.back: The sequence of events that make up a story, arranged by the writer so that one event leads to the next.
cards.note: Plot is what happens; setting and character are where and to whom.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is exposition in a plot?
cards.back: The opening part of a story that introduces the characters, the setting and the background before the main trouble begins.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the climax of a story?
cards.back: The turning point at which the tension is highest and the main conflict reaches its peak, so the outcome is about to be decided.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the resolution of a plot?
cards.back: The part in which the main conflict is settled and the story's problem is solved or ends.
cards.note: Many glossaries use 'denouement' for this closing part of the plot.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the denouement of a story?
cards.back: The final part after the climax, in which the remaining threads are drawn together and the outcome is made clear.
cards.note: The word comes from French, meaning 'untying' (of a knot).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is conflict in a story?
cards.back: A struggle between opposing forces, such as two characters or a character and something outside, that drives the plot.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an internal conflict?
cards.back: A struggle inside a character's own mind, such as between desire and duty, or between two choices.
cards.note: Example: a boy torn between telling the truth and shielding his friend.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an external conflict?
cards.back: A struggle between a character and something outside himself or herself, such as another person, nature or society.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Who is the protagonist of a story?
cards.back: The main character, around whom the story centres and whose struggle the reader mainly follows.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Who is the antagonist of a story?
cards.back: The character or force that opposes the protagonist and creates the main conflict.
cards.note: An antagonist need not be a villain; it may be a rival, a group or a force.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a foil in a story?
cards.back: A character who contrasts sharply with another, usually the main character, so that the other's qualities stand out.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is characterisation?
cards.back: The way a writer creates and presents a character, through description, speech, actions and what others say or think.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is direct characterisation?
cards.back: The writer or narrator tells the reader plainly what a character is like.
cards.note: Example: Meera was a generous, impatient girl.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is indirect characterisation?
cards.back: The reader learns what a character is like from the character's speech, actions and thoughts and from other people's reactions, not from a plain statement.
cards.note: Example: Meera pressed her lunch into the beggar's hands and ran for the bus.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a round character?
cards.back: A complex, fully developed character with many sides, strengths and flaws, who can surprise the reader.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a flat character?
cards.back: A simple character built around one quality or idea, who shows little depth and rarely surprises the reader.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a dynamic character?
cards.back: A character who changes in an important way, such as in attitude or understanding, because of the events of the story.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a static character?
cards.back: A character who stays basically the same from the beginning to the end of the story.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the setting of a story?
cards.back: The time and place in which a story happens, often with its social surroundings.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the theme of a story?
cards.back: The central idea or underlying message about life or human nature that a story explores.
cards.note: A theme is usually shown through events and characters, not announced.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is the moral of a story?
cards.back: The lesson about right and wrong or good conduct that a story teaches, often stated at its end.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is mood in a story?
cards.back: The feeling or atmosphere that a piece of writing creates in the reader, such as gloom, calm or tension.
cards.note: Setting, description and word choice help to build it.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is point of view in a narrative?
cards.back: The position from which a story is told, decided by who tells it and how much that teller knows.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is first-person narration?
cards.back: A narrator who is part of the story tells it as 'I' (or 'we'), so the reader sees events only through that person's eyes.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is third-person omniscient narration?
cards.back: An outside narrator, using 'he', 'she' and 'they', who knows the thoughts and feelings of all the characters and the events everywhere.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is third-person limited narration?
cards.back: An outside narrator, using 'he' or 'she', who tells the story through the thoughts and feelings of one character only.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an unreliable narrator?
cards.back: A narrator whose account the reader cannot fully trust, because he or she is mistaken, biased, dishonest or too young to understand.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a flashback in a narrative?
cards.back: A scene that breaks into the story's present to show something that happened earlier.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is foreshadowing?
cards.back: Hints or clues given early in a story that suggest what will happen later.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is suspense in a story?
cards.back: The tense, excited uncertainty a reader feels about what will happen next, especially to a character in danger.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a cliffhanger?
cards.back: An ending, or the end of a chapter, that stops at an exciting moment with the outcome unsettled, so the reader wants to read on.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an anecdote?
cards.back: A short, interesting or amusing account of a real incident, usually about a person.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a fable?
cards.back: A short story, often with animals as characters, that teaches a moral lesson.
cards.note: Example: the tale of the tortoise and the hare.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a parable?
cards.back: A short, simple story about people that teaches a moral or spiritual lesson.
cards.note: Unlike a fable, a parable usually has human characters.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is an epiphany in literature?
cards.back: A sudden moment in which a character grasps a truth or sees something in a new light.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: What is a character's motive in a story?
cards.back: The reason that makes a character act as he or she does, such as a want, a fear or a need.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Stages of a plot, in order
cards.back:
Exposition: the characters, setting and background are introduced.
Rising action: events build the conflict and the tension.
Climax: the turning point, where the tension is highest.
Falling action: events after the climax lead towards the end.
Resolution: the conflict is settled and the story closes.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Types of conflict in a story
cards.back:
Person vs person: a character struggles against another character.
Person vs self: a character struggles with his or her own doubts or choices.
Person vs nature: a character struggles against a natural force, such as a storm or the wilderness.
Person vs society: a character struggles against the rules, customs or beliefs of a group.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Types of point of view in a narrative
cards.back:
First person: a character tells the story as 'I'.
Second person: the narrator speaks to 'you'; this is rare in stories.
Third-person omniscient: an outside narrator knows every character's mind.
Third-person limited: an outside narrator shows one character's mind only.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Types of character in a story
cards.back:
Round: complex and fully developed, with many sides.
Flat: simple, built around one quality.
Dynamic: changes because of the events of the story.
Static: stays the same from beginning to end.
cards.note: Round and flat describe depth; dynamic and static describe change.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Theme vs moral: the difference
cards.back:
Theme: the central idea or message a story explores, often put in a phrase (for example, the cost of greed).
Moral: a direct lesson on how to behave, often stated as a sentence (for example, 'Greed brings ruin').

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Theme vs topic: the difference
cards.back:
Topic: the subject the story is about, in a word or phrase (for example, friendship).
Theme: what the story says about that subject, as a full statement (for example, true friends stand by you in hard times).

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Flashback vs foreshadowing: the difference
cards.back:
Flashback: shows an event from the past, breaking into the present of the story.
Foreshadowing: hints at an event that has not yet happened.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: First-person vs third-person narration: the difference
cards.back:
First person: the narrator is a character in the story and says 'I', so the view is limited to that character.
Third person: the narrator stands outside the story and uses 'he', 'she' and 'they'.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Round vs flat character: the difference
cards.back:
Round: complex, with strengths and flaws, and able to surprise the reader.
Flat: simple, shown by one trait, and easy to predict.

cards.subject: english
cards.front: Dynamic vs static character: the difference
cards.back:
Dynamic: changes in attitude or understanding during the story.
